title: How to update your e‑commerce catalog without re-editing every image
summary: Learn how to bulk edit product images across your e‑commerce catalog, update backgrounds and formats, and keep existing product imagery consistent.
body_markdown:
Changing one product image is quick. Changing the same thing across 500 product images isn't.


Maybe you've updated your product image background. Your marketplace requires different dimensions. Older listings don't match newer photography. Or you want consistent positioning, padding, and shadows across a product catalog built over several years.


The instinct is often to start opening images and fixing them. But if the same change affects hundreds of assets, **you don't have hundreds of image-editing problems. You have one rule that needs to change across the catalog.**


Instead of editing hundreds of images one-by-one, a more efficient process is:


**Identify what changed → define the new rule → apply it in bulk → review exceptions → republish**


That lets you update an existing e‑commerce catalog without turning every refresh into another product photography project. This is where Photoroom fits: helping sellers edit e‑commerce product images—from[removing backgrounds](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/background-remover) to[resizing images](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/image-resizer) or[changing product positioning](https://www.photoroom.com/batch/align-product-photos) —across[hundreds of images at once](https://www.photoroom.com/batch) .


## Table of Contents


## 1. Identify if the product or presentation changed


Before editing anything, determine what actually changed between when you first created the image and now. There is an important difference between **changing the product** and **changing how the product is presented** .


If the product itself has changed, you may need a new source image. Examples of a product change include:


-


New packaging


-


A redesigned label


-


A physical design change


-


A different material


-


An actual new color


-


A feature that needs to be visible


But many catalog updates don't change the product at all. You may simply need:


-


A different background


-


New image dimensions


-


More consistent cropping


-


Different padding


-


Standardized product positioning


-


A new shadow treatment


-


Marketplace-specific formatting


-


A seasonal or branded presentation


In those cases, reshooting or rebuilding the product image from scratch can create unnecessary work.


**If the product remains accurate, reuse the product asset and change the presentation around it.**


That distinction becomes increasingly important as your[catalog grows](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-scale-product-image-creation-e-commerce) .


## 2. Define the new rule before editing the first image


Say you want every primary product image to have a white background. You could open the first image, remove its background, replace it, export the result, and move to the next one. Before doing that 500 times, define what the complete finished image should actually look like.


For example:


-


Background: white


-


Dimensions: 2000 × 2000 px


-


Product position: centered


-


Product scale: consistent within the frame


-


Padding: 10%


-


Shadow: soft and consistent


-


Output: JPEG


Now that you’ve made those choices once, you don’t have to make them for every product image. You've created one visual rule that can be applied[repeatedly across the entire product catalog](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-create-repeatable-product-image-workflow) .


The same principle works for various types of catalog updates:


-


**If**[marketplace requirements](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/multichannel-product-image-optimization) **change** , define the new dimensions and composition once.


-


**If your brand changes its product-image style** , define the new background, crop, positioning, and shadow treatment before updating individual products.


-


**If old supplier images don't match newer photography** , establish what the finished catalog should look like first.


**If the change can be expressed as a rule, it shouldn't have to be manually reinvented for every image.**


## 3. Identify which product images actually need to be updated


A catalog refresh doesn't necessarily mean updating every image. Before bulk editing product images, identify which assets are actually affected.


Maybe only:


-


Primary listing images use the old background


-


One product category has inconsistent crops


-


Products from a particular supplier use outdated imagery


-


Older SKUs use the previous template


-


One marketplace needs a new format


-


One image type needs different dimensions


Segmenting the catalog first prevents unnecessary work and reduces the risk of changing assets that are already correct.


This is particularly useful for stores that have grown over time. A catalog might contain images from several photography workflows: original studio shoots, supplier assets, internal photography, older templates, and newer AI-assisted production. They don't necessarily need the same fix. So, define the problem first. Then select the products affected by it.


## 4. Apply repeatable changes to product images in bulk


Once you've defined the new image standard and identified the affected assets,[repeatable changes can be applied together](https://www.photoroom.com/batch) instead of image by image.


Common bulk product image edits include:


-


[Removing backgrounds](https://www.photoroom.com/batch/background-remover)


-


[Replacing backgrounds](https://www.photoroom.com/batch/ai-backgrounds)


-


[Resizing](https://www.photoroom.com/batch/image-resizer)


-


[Repositioning products](https://www.photoroom.com/batch/align-product-photos)


-


Adjusting padding


-


[Applying templates](https://www.photoroom.com/templates)


-


[Adding shadows](https://www.photoroom.com/batch/ai-shadows)


-


Standardizing image dimensions


Instead of:


**image → edit → export → repeat**


the workflow becomes:


**define rule → apply across selected images → review**


With[Photoroom's Batch Mode](https://www.photoroom.com/batch) , you can import multiple product images and apply common edits across them rather than recreating the same treatment for every individual file. This is particularly useful when the underlying product imagery is still accurate and the change only affects how products are presented. You can then save a collection of edits—for example, remove background, add shadows, and adjust padding—as a[template](https://www.photoroom.com/templates) to standardize future product photography, too.


The value of batch editing isn't simply doing the same manual work faster. It's removing the need to make that decision 500 times instead of once. Photoroom users agree: across a selection of 1,356 Photoroom users in the UK,[40% use batch editing](https://www.photoroom.com/industry-trends/product-photography-cost-for-smbs) —whether they’re shipping dozens of products from a spare room, or managing a warehouse’s worth of product catalog imagery.


### When should you bulk edit product images?


Bulk editing makes sense when the **same predictable change applies to multiple existing images.**


Examples of when to edit product images in bulk include:


Catalog change Bulk-edit approach


New background standard Replace backgrounds across affected assets


New image dimensions Resize selected product images


Inconsistent positioning Apply consistent scale and positioning


New shadow treatment Apply a standard shadow


Updated marketplace requirements Create the required format across eligible products


Legacy imagery Bring older assets into the current visual standard


New brand treatment Apply the updated template to relevant products


Bulk editing is less appropriate when the underlying products themselves have changed or when every image requires a fundamentally different creative decision.


When considering bulk editing, instead of asking:


**Can these images be edited faster?**


Ask:


**Does this change follow a rule that can be applied reliably across multiple assets?**


If the answer is yes, the task is a strong candidate for[bulk editing](https://www.photoroom.com/batch) .


## 5. Keep the product accurate


Bulk editing can make a catalog more consistent, but consistency shouldn't come at the expense of product accuracy. When updating existing product imagery, distinguish between the elements you're deliberately changing and the details that should remain untouched.


Check important product characteristics such as:


-


Color


-


Shape


-


Proportions


-


Materials


-


Textures


-


Logos


-


Labels


-


Patterns


-


Distinctive details


This matters particularly when AI is used to create new backgrounds, scenes, shadows, or other presentations.


When thinking about product accuracy, a useful rule is:


**Change the presentation deliberately. Preserve the product faithfully.**


That lets you refresh an existing catalog without turning a visual update into a product-representation problem.


## 6. Review exceptions instead of rebuilding every image manually


Bulk editing doesn't mean blindly approving every output. Products may generate inconsistent results even when put through the same editing process. For example, a standard background-removal or positioning rule that works perfectly for most of a catalog may struggle with:


-


Transparent products


-


Reflective materials


-


Unusually shaped items


-


Complex edges


-


Low-quality source images


-


Products photographed at unusual angles


These exceptions don't mean you should avoid automation. Instead, design the workflow around them. If a rule works for 190 out of 200 images, direct human attention should focus on the ten that require intervention.


The workflow becomes:


**apply rule → identify exceptions → fix exceptions**


rather than:


**Manually rebuilding 200 images when only ten are difficult**


This approach reflects how AI changes the role of human review in product photography. Instead of performing every standard production task manually, people can focus on[product accuracy](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-fix-inaccurate-ai-product-images) , unusual outputs, and cases where judgment genuinely matters.


## How to fix inconsistency across the product catalog


Catalog refreshes can be an opportunity to address inconsistencies that have accumulated over time. A growing e‑commerce store rarely creates all of its imagery at once:


-


Products may have been photographed years apart.


-


Different suppliers may provide different source assets.


-


Newer products may follow visual standards that didn't exist when older listings were created.


The result can be a catalog where:


-


Product scale changes from listing to listing


-


Backgrounds vary slightly


-


Shadows appear on some products but not others


-


Crops are inconsistent


-


Padding varies


-


Older images look noticeably different from newer ones


Fixing those issues one image at a time can make[catalog consistency](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-create-consistent-product-images-across-categories) feel permanently out of reach. Instead, define the visual standard you want the catalog to follow and identify which existing assets fall outside the visual standard. Then apply the new standard across the entire selection of images that fall outside the standard, either using[batch editing](https://www.photoroom.com/batch) or manual edits for products that require human review.


With this approach, the refresh becomes a standardization project rather than a collection of unrelated image fixes.


## How to update product images when channel requirements change


Your catalog imagery needs to evolve when you expand to new channels, too. The product itself may remain identical, but the required visual asset usually changes.


Your e‑commerce store, a marketplace, product feed, an advertising platform, and social media may each require different:


-


Dimensions


-


Aspect ratios


-


Backgrounds


-


Crops


-


Compositions


-


File formats


That doesn't mean every new channel needs another complete product photography workflow. Where the underlying product image remains accurate, use it as a baseline to[create the channel-specific output](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/multichannel-product-image-optimization) .


Instead of:


**new channel → new product photography**


The model becomes:


**reliable product asset → channel-specific presentations**


Additionally, this model makes future updates easier. If requirements change again, you're updating the output rules rather than recreating the product image itself.


## How to bulk update Shopify product images without rebuilding the upload workflow


Bulk image editing is only one part of a catalog update. The other part is getting every finished asset back to the correct product.


A traditional workflow might look like:


**download → organize → edit → export → rename → find product → upload → assign image**


But when you're updating hundreds of existing listings, those handoffs can become a significant part of the workload. The closer image production is to the catalog itself, the fewer manual steps each update creates.


For Shopify sellers,[Photoroom's Shopify integration](https://www.photoroom.com/integrations/shopify) lets you access Shopify products and their existing images inside Photoroom, batch edit product imagery, and publish changes back to Shopify. That reduces the need to create another download-edit-upload process around the catalog refresh.


## How to update an existing e‑commerce catalog with a simple workflow


When you need to refresh product imagery across an existing catalog, follow five steps.


### 1. Identify what changed


Determine whether the product itself changed or only its visual presentation.


### 2. Define the new rule


Specify the background, dimensions, crop, position, padding, shadow, format, or other requirement.


### 3. Segment affected assets


Update only the products and images that actually need the change.


### 4. Apply the update in bulk


Use[batch editing](https://www.photoroom.com/batch) tools,[templates](https://www.photoroom.com/templates) , or other repeatable processes rather than recreating the edit independently.


### 5. Review exceptions and republish


[Check product accuracy](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-fix-inaccurate-ai-product-images) and unusual outputs, then return approved assets to the correct listings.


The important part happens before editing begins. **When your catalog changes, don't start with the images. Start with the rule that changed.** Once that rule is clear, the work becomes much easier to apply systematically.


## Update the rule, not every image


E‑commerce catalogs aren't static. Brands evolve. Marketplaces change their requirements. New channels appear. Visual standards improve. And older imagery eventually stops matching the rest of the store. That doesn't mean every change should trigger another manual editing project.


**A catalog-wide image change should be one rule change, not hundreds of individual editing decisions.**


If the underlying product remains accurate, keep the product asset and update the presentation around it. Define the new standard once. Apply it to the assets that need it. Review the exceptions. Then publish the updated catalog.


With Photoroom, you can complete these steps in a single workflow. Define your visual standard,[apply it across the relevant products](https://www.photoroom.com/batch) , review exceptions, and[publish new images directly to your Shopify storefront](https://www.photoroom.com/integrations/shopify) . The value isn’t just making updates faster—it’s making visual consistency a single project.
